content: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a common joint condition characterized by the breakdown of cartilage, leading to pain and decreased mobility. Nutrition has emerged as an important modifiable factor influencing osteoarthritis symptoms and potentially its progression. Major mechanisms include the effects of body weight on joint loading, dietary patterns influencing systemic inflammation, and nutrient impacts on cartilage health. Excess weight increases mechanical stress on weight-bearing joints such as knees and hips, often worsening symptoms and accelerating cartilage degradation. Hence, weight management through appropriate diet is essential. Certain foods rich in antioxidants and omega-3 fatty acids may reduce low-grade inflammation linked to OA, though evidence on dietary interventions directly altering OA progression is emergent and not conclusive. Quality of diet — including adequate intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats — also contributes to overall joint health and symptom management. Practical relevance lies in individualized nutrition counseling that balances weight control, nutrient adequacy, and anti-inflammatory dietary components. However, limitations include variability in clinical trial results and the complexity of OA pathogenesis. Important related concepts include the role of systemic inflammation, the impact of micronutrients such as vitamin D and C, and lifestyle factors alongside diet. Nutrition should be considered a complementary component of OA management rather than a standalone treatment.

content: Osteoarthritis (OA) affects millions worldwide, primarily impacting cartilage and the surrounding joint structures. Nutrition is relevant because body weight directly affects joint load, and diet influences systemic inflammation and nutrient availability for joint repair. Appreciating this connection supports holistic management strategies.

chunk_title: Impact of Weight Management on Osteoarthritis
content: Excess body weight increases mechanical stress on joints, especially weight-bearing ones like knees and hips. This stress accelerates cartilage wear and intensifies pain and disability. Weight loss of even 5-10% body weight can significantly reduce symptoms and improve function. Nutrition plays a central role in achieving and maintaining a healthy weight.

content: A balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats supplies antioxidants and phytochemicals that can combat oxidative damage in joint tissues. Adequate nutrition supports cartilage metabolism and general musculoskeletal health, which may help mitigate osteoarthritis symptoms.

chunk_title: Fatty Acids: Types and Effects on Osteoarthritis
content: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids found in fish oil have been studied for their potential to reduce joint inflammation and stiffness. Conversely, excessive intake of omega-6 fatty acids or saturated fats may promote inflammation. Balancing fat intake is a nutritional target for improving osteoarthritis outcomes.

content: Supplements such as glucosamine, chondroitin, and omega-3 fatty acids are popular among people with osteoarthritis. Evidence on their benefits is mixed, with some studies suggesting symptom relief but limited impact on disease progression. Patients should discuss supplements with healthcare providers.
